newsitem.title: FRANCE: Giscard slams French summit achievements.
newsitem.headline: Giscard slams French summit achievements.

text.p: Ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing on Friday harshly criticised France's performance at a string of recent high-stakes international summits, dismissing them as failures for Paris.
"Amsterdam was negative. Denver was useless. Madrid was a disappointment for France," he said in an interview in the daily Le Monde.

Little progress was made on reforming European Union institutions at last month's Amsterdam EU summit while a Denver meeting of leaders of the Group of Seven industrialised nations plus Russia had no discernible results at all, he said.

As for this week's NATO summit in Madrid, France had failed to win alliance membership for its two candidates, Romania and Slovenia, and also failed to achieve its goal of reforms enabling it to return to NATO's military command, he said.
At the G7 meeting, "we don't even know what happened there. It was clear from the published statement that the participants had not had the time to either edit or read it."

Giscard d'Estaing, founder of the centre-right Union for French Democracy, who was head of state from 1974 until 1981, seemed to blame both the new leftist government and conservative President Jacques Chirac for France's woes.
He accused Chirac of ignoring his policy advice and said the left's ideas reflected "a vision of the past" which would prevent France from modernising.

In a slap at his own political allies, he said Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin had responded better than the previous centre-right government to voter concerns expressed in the June 1 parliamentary election won by the left.
Giscard d'Estaing said the French constitution compounded the right's problem now that it was in opposition by weakening the president's powers.
He called for a reform of the constitution "at the appropriate time", with a referendum to shorten the presidential term to five years from seven.

Giscard d'Estaing, who remains a member of parliament but no longer holds a party leadership post, has criticised Chirac several times in recent months although both are part of the same centre-right camp.
He publicly criticised Chirac's dissolution of parliament before the right's election defeat, saying the president would have been wiser simply to change policy.
